messages.author: 4cacbe3a86a908bf
messages.subject: Re: Comparing densities obtained from different models
parts:
Hi Harriet, List,

There should be no problem at all in comparing two independent estimates=20
with different detection function models, given that the distance=20
sampling assumptions hold in both instances. Since each estimate is then=20
an unbiased estimate (with a precision measure associated with it), and=20
these are independent, the comparison is straightforward.

As you say, given that the same data is used, a negative exponential=20
model tends to lead to higher estimates than the half normal say. But=20
that in itself is not an issue. What is an issue, and one that maybe you=20
need to think about, is why did you get the negative exponential to be=20
selected by AIC in the first place. I guess in most cases in which the=20
negative exponential is selected based on AIC it is so because there was=20
a problem in the data rather than it representing the true detection=20
function.

Do you have spiked data? If so, why are the data spiked? Is there an=20
assumption violation going on? Do you have too many 0 distances in your=20
data?

Your solution to force the same model to these 2 data sets is not=20
reasonable, because you do not need at all to have the same model to=20
make proper comparisons. In fact, in many cases you will have different=20
models across different species, but that just tells you that these=20
species have different detection functions. Fitting the same model, say=20
the half normal, will probably mean the kudu estimates become lower, but=20
it will not mean that the new estimate is better than the old one. What=20
you need to do first is to understand why the data was spiked to=20
beguin with, to then be able to act accordingly.

Hope this helps,

Tiago
